newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Eramet shares hit by Pacific nickel mine row.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Eramet shares hit by Pacific nickel mine row.

text.p: Shares in France's Eramet SA, the world's third-biggest nickel producer, slid on Monday after the government said it had started moves to withdraw the firm's nickel mining licence for Koniambo in New Caledonia.

The French government, claiming Eramet had not exploited the mine since 1975, wants to hand the concession to local Kanak interests on the South Pacific island so that the ore can be used in a new nickel smelter.
The smelter project is part of a deal to appease Kanaks ahead of a 1998 referendum on independence among the 197,000 people on the island, 18,000 kms from mainland France.
Eramet shares in Paris were trading 8.5 percent down at 280 francs at 1215 GMT.

The Industry Ministry said that a 1954 mining decree contained the possibility of expropriation if the Koniambo mine was not exploited for more than 10 years. It said it had started the administrative procedure to withdraw the mining lincence.
"The government will see to it that the patrimonial interests of Eramet will not be hurt," the ministry said.

In a statement, Eramet said it would use all legal means in its possession to prevent the disappropriation, which it said would cause it "considerable prejudice" and would affect its financial outlook.

The company said it believed that under current laws and regulations in New Caledonia such a decision could not be justified. Eramet's Societe Le Nickel (SLN) has been operating the mine for more than a century and plans to increase production.
A government official said the state had taken the decision to start the Koniambo expropriation after talks between SLN and Kanak Societe Miniere du Sud Pacifique (SMSP) over an asset swap failed.
"The companies could not agree amongst each other because the SMSP wanted a deal with immediate effect," the official said.
Eramet could lose the licence within four months and because the it was given freely Eramet would not receive compensation under the original letter of agreement.
However, the government plans to start separate talks over compensation.

Some investment funds, such as Fidelity, have warned the government of the possible consequences on, for example, the sale of France Telecom shares, if France did not respect the interests of Eramet minorities.

On January 30, the French government and officials of the two main political parties of the French South Pacific island of New Caledonia agreed to re-allocate mining reserves within the territory so that local Kanak independence groups could go ahead with plans to build a nickel plant in the north.
Under the plan, Canadian group Falconbridge and the SMPS would get the right to use the Koniambo field while Eramet would obtain rights to the Poum field.

Eramet, 55 percent owned by the state, also owns the Thiebaghi mines which are crucial for its explansion plans to produce over 60,000 tonnes of nickel by the year 2000 from a 1996 output level of 56,000 tonnes, made out of some three million tonnes of nickel ore.

The preliminary January agreement was concluded between French officials and Socialist Liberation Front (FLNKS) president Rock Wamytan as well as the anti-independence Rally for a Republican Caledonia, linked to the Gaulist Rally for the Republic (RPR) party of French president Jacques Chirac.

The referendum promise was part of a 1988 deal which followed the "Ouvea Cave" incident in which 19 Kanaks and three gendarmes were killed and which formed the climax of years of bloody strife. France colonised New Caldeonia in 1853.
